title: Spin or sleep
sub: SpinWait and SpinLock vs Mutex, Semaphore and kernel events
cards/0/body:
The lock is taken. What should a thread do?

  • Spin: check in a loop whether it was released. The thread stays in user mode, keeps its quantum and reacts within nanoseconds. But all that time it burns a CPU core for nothing.
  • Sleep in the OS kernel: ask the scheduler to take the thread off the CPU and wake it on a signal. The core is free for others. But the switch to kernel mode and back, the context switch and the wake-up cost a few microseconds, and the woken thread still waits for its turn.

Hence the rule: spinning pays off only if the wait will be shorter than the cost of falling asleep and waking up, and there is a second core on which the lock owner is running right now.
cards/1/q: When is pure spinning worse than sleeping in the kernel?
cards/1/options/0: The lock owner was preempted and is not running: the waiter burns its quantum until it comes back
cards/1/options/1: The lock is held for 50 nanoseconds on a 16-core machine
cards/1/options/2: The critical section is a single assignment
cards/1/explain: While the owner is not running, nobody can release the lock — spinning is guaranteed to be useless. On a single core it is the worst case: the spinning thread itself keeps the owner from getting the CPU. The other options are exactly the good cases for spinning.
cards/2/title: SpinWait: a spin that knows when to stop
cards/2/body:
Writing while (!flag) { } by hand is bad: endless starvation on one core, extra heat and interference with the sibling hyperthread on many. The SpinWait struct does it right:

  • the first SpinOnce() calls really spin, with a hint instruction to the CPU (pause on x64) and a growing iteration count;
  • after about ten calls it starts yielding the CPU: Thread.Yield, Sleep(0), sometimes Sleep(1);
  • on a single-core machine it yields right away.

NextSpinWillYield tells you it is time to switch to a real wait. A ready-made wrapper is SpinWait.SpinUntil(condition, timeout).
cards/3/title: SpinLock — a struct with sharp edges
cards/3/body:
SpinLock is a lock that spins under contention using that same SpinWait. It allocates no objects and never sleeps on a kernel object — on a long wait it merely yields its quantum through that same SpinWait — so it suits critical sections of a few instructions that are taken very often.

You enter with Enter(ref bool lockTaken). The method sets lockTaken = true exactly at the moment the lock is taken, and finally releases only what was really taken. That is why Enter sits inside try: if something fails before the lock is acquired, Exit is not called on a lock you do not hold. The compiler expands every lock into the same shape — Monitor.Enter(obj, ref lockTaken) inside try; why it was invented is covered in the next lesson.

The sharp edges:

  • it is a struct: a copy is a separate lock. Do not pass it by value and do not keep it in a readonly field. For a readonly field the compiler calls a mutating method on a temporary copy (a defensive copy): _spin.Enter takes the copy, the field itself stays free — there is no mutual exclusion;
  • it is not reentrant: re-entering on the same thread throws LockRecursionException with owner tracking, and spins forever without it.

Rule: start with lock. Move to SpinLock only if the profiler showed that this particular lock is hot.
cards/4/q: Under load items get lost, even though every write is under the SpinLock. Which line is to blame?
cards/4/explain: Calling a method on a struct in a readonly field works on a defensive copy: each Enter takes its own temporary lock, and there is no mutual exclusion. Remove readonly — then Enter changes the field itself.
cards/5/body:
Mutex, Semaphore, EventWaitHandle (and its children AutoResetEvent, ManualResetEvent) wrap OS objects. All of them derive from WaitHandle and hold a kernel handle.

  • The cost: on Windows every WaitOne, Set, Release is a system call, even when there was nothing to wait for. On Linux and macOS the runtime emulates these objects in its own layer, with no system call on a free object, but the path is still long. Either way it is tens of times more expensive than entering a free lock.
  • The strength: an object can have a name, and then other processes see it. On Windows all three types can be named. On Linux and macOS the runtime supports a name only on Mutex: a named Semaphore or EventWaitHandle throws PlatformNotSupportedException there. Plus WaitHandle.WaitAny/WaitAll — wait on several objects at once.

Cross-process synchronization is the main reason to use them today. Inside one process there is almost always a lightweight replacement: lock, SemaphoreSlim, ManualResetEventSlim.
cards/5/deep:
On Windows the Global\ prefix makes a name visible across all sessions, Local\ (the default) only within your own.

WaitHandle still derives from MarshalByRefObject — a legacy of .NET Framework, where it also served to synchronize across application domains (AppDomain). Modern .NET has no extra application domains, so that base class gives nothing.
cards/6/title: Events and the semaphore: who closes and who releases
cards/6/body:
An event is a flag in the kernel with two states: signaled (open) and non-signaled (closed). WaitOne on an open event passes at once, on a closed one it sleeps until the event is opened. The two kinds differ in who closes it:

  • ManualResetEvent works like a gate. Set() opens it, and everyone passes — all the waiters and everyone who comes later — until someone calls Reset(). Good for a "ready" signal to many at once.
  • AutoResetEvent works like a turnstile. One Set() lets one waiter through, and the event closes by itself. If nobody is waiting, the signal stays until the first WaitOne. An event has a single state, so two Set calls in a row with no waiters give one pass, not two.
  • Semaphore is a counter of free slots in the kernel. WaitOne takes a slot or sleeps while there are none; Release() returns a slot. A semaphore has no owner, so any thread may call Release, not only the one that took the slot. You cannot go over the maximum: an extra Release throws SemaphoreFullException.

Compared to SemaphoreSlim from the pitfalls unit, Semaphore lives in the kernel (and can be named) and has no WaitAsync: its WaitOne always blocks the thread.
cards/7/q: Three threads wait in WaitOne() on one AutoResetEvent. Another thread calls Set() once. What happens?
cards/7/options/0: One thread wakes up, the event closes again
cards/7/options/2: One wakes up, the event stays open
cards/7/options/3: None: Set has no effect without Reset
cards/7/explain: One Set, one pass: the first waiter goes through, AutoResetEvent closes again by itself, and the other two keep sleeping. A ManualResetEvent would let all three through after Set — and everyone after them until Reset.
cards/8/title: Mutex: the owner and the abandoned lock
cards/8/body:
A Mutex remembers its owning thread. Only the thread that took it may release it: ReleaseMutex from another thread throws ApplicationException. So, as with lock, an await between acquire and release is a bug.

It is reentrant: the owner may take it again, but must release it the same number of times.

If the owning thread or process died without releasing the mutex, the OS hands it to the next waiter, who gets an AbandonedMutexException. The lock is already theirs, but the data under it may be half-modified.

The classic use is "only one instance of the program":
cards/9/q: Prevent a second instance of the program from starting
cards/9/explain: You need an object other processes can see — a named Mutex. The last parameter tells whether we created it (the first instance) or opened an existing one. SemaphoreSlim and Monitor live only inside one process.
cards/10/q: Match the primitive with its trait
cards/10/pairs/0/1: Tied to the owning thread, can be cross-process
cards/10/pairs/1/1: A counter in the kernel, any thread may release it
cards/10/pairs/2/1: Set lets one waiter through and closes
cards/10/pairs/3/1: After Set it is open for everyone until Reset
cards/10/pairs/4/1: A struct, waits in user mode
cards/11/options/0: On Windows every WaitOne on a Mutex is a system call, even if the mutex is free
cards/11/options/1: A Semaphore can be released from another thread
cards/11/options/3: SpinWait on a single-core machine yields the CPU right away
cards/11/options/4: A named Semaphore works on Linux the same way as on Windows
cards/11/explain: SpinLock is not reentrant — unlike Monitor and Mutex. On Linux and macOS only mutexes can be named; for Semaphore and EventWaitHandle names are supported on Windows only.
